title: Why Coming On Too Strong Will Force A Mutiny In Your Classroom ny-in-your-classroom/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin challenges the common belief that teachers must adopt a tough, intimidating posture to establish classroom management, arguing that fear-based approaches consistently backfire. He lists several specific harms of coming on too strong: it creates an us-against-them mentality, frames classroom management negatively, boxes teachers into a punitive persona, damages likability, and undermines the rapport and influence needed for real behavior change. He contends that presenting a classroom management plan through detailed modeling, role-play, and practice — rather than through threats and toughness — allows teachers to remain themselves while being far more effective, both immediately and over the long term.
points: Coming on too strong when introducing classroom management creates an 'us-against-them' dynamic before the plan is even in place.
An aggressive, new-sheriff-in-town posture frames classroom management as something negative to resist rather than a benefit to embrace.
Establishing a tough persona early forces a teacher to maintain it all year, since inconsistency between toughness and calm enforcement undermines credibility.
Being seen as 'mean' damages the likability that is essential for building rapport and influence with students.
Teaching classroom management through detailed modeling, role-play, and practice is more effective, in both the short and long term, than trying to intimidate students into compliance.
quotes: Fear and intimidation belong in the dark ages of classroom management. The truth is, you can’t force today’s students into behaving.
The moment you crossover from being seen as the trusted leader to being viewed as an antagonist or enemy, bad things begin to happen.
Coming on too strong will force you to behave similarly whenever you have to deal with misbehavior. Otherwise, your students won’t take you seriously.
I’ve heard teachers claim that they don’t mind if students dislike them. This may be true, but when your students don’t like you, your ability to build rapport and influence goes down the drain.

When your focus is on teaching classroom management—through detailed modeling, role-play, and practice—rather than trying to convince students through your tough-as-nails posture that you really mean it, you’re free to be yourself, even have fun while presenting your plan.
